meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Silence is a source of great strength'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Lao Tzu, but the words are John Heider's, from his 1985 book The Tao of Leadership. It is not in the Tao Te Ching.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — actually John Heider
answer.authorDates: 1936–2010 · American clinical psychologist & Human Potential Movement figure
answer.sourceLine: The line does not come from Lao Tzu or the Tao Te Ching. It is a lightly reworded version of “Silence is a great source of strength,” written by John Heider in The Tao of Leadership: Lao Tzu’s Tao Te Ching Adapted for a New Age ↗ (Humanics New Age, 1985) — a book Heider described as his own modern adaptation, not a translation. The viral form swaps his phrasing to “a source of great strength.”

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: The leader does not gossip about others or waste breath arguing the merits of competing theories. Silence is a great source of strength.
trail: The line is attributed to Lao Tzu across quote aggregators such as BrainyQuote ↗ and Goodreads ↗, but none cites a chapter of the Tao Te Ching.
Taoism author Stefan Stenudd lists it among his catalogue of fake Lao Tzu quotes ↗, noting it is “not really Lao Tzu’s own words” and tracing it to John Heider’s adaptation.
The words “Silence is a great source of strength” are recorded as John Heider’s, from The Tao of Leadership ↗, where they close a passage on leaders who do not gossip or argue.
source.excerptNote: Heider’s original wording in The Tao of Leadership (1985). The popular meme reorders it to “Silence is a source of great strength” and re-credits it to Lao Tzu.

source.rightsHolder: Estate of John Heider / Humanics Publishing Group
source.rightsNote: The displayed wording derives from John Heider’s The Tao of Leadership (Humanics New Age, 1985), a modern adaptation by an identifiable author who died in 2010; it is therefore protected by copyright, not public domain. The ancient Tao Te Ching itself is public domain, but this specific English aphorism is Heider’s twentieth-century creation, not a passage from that text.

author.name: John Heider
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: 1936–2010 · American clinical psychologist & Human Potential Movement figure
author.bio: John Heider (1936–2010) was an American clinical psychologist and a seminal figure in the Human Potential Movement, who worked at the Esalen Institute and founded the Human Potential School of Mendocino. His 1985 book The Tao of Leadership reimagines the Tao Te Ching as a handbook for group facilitators and managers; Heider was explicit that it was “his own version of the meaning of Lao Tzu’s words,” not a scholarly translation. Many of its crisp modern lines — including this one — have since been stripped of his name and recirculated as if they were ancient sayings of Lao Tzu.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a classic case of a modern author’s words being back-dated to an ancient sage. The sentiment sounds Taoist, but the sentence is not Lao Tzu’s.

items.why: Quote sites and social media credit the line to Lao Tzu, yet it appears in no translation of the Tao Te Ching. Taoism specialist Stefan Stenudd files it under fake Lao Tzu quotes ↗, concluding it is “really not” Lao Tzu’s own words.

The wording is Heider’s, from The Tao of Leadership (1985) ↗: “Silence is a great source of strength.” Heider presented the whole book as his own adaptation of Taoist ideas for a modern audience, not a translation — and the meme reorders even his phrasing.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are John Heider’s 1985 paraphrase of Taoist themes, not a saying of Lao Tzu — and even the popular form (“a source of great strength”) alters Heider’s own line ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The Tao Te Ching genuinely prizes stillness and restraint — Chapter 56 opens “Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know” — so a crisp aphorism linking silence to strength feels authentically Taoist. That plausibility is exactly what lets a modern line pass as ancient.

John Heider built The Tao of Leadership on that resonance, translating Lao Tzu’s themes into brisk advice for group leaders. His memorable phrasing travelled so well that it outran his name, landing back on the sage it was inspired by.
detailsBody: Heider’s book has been reprinted for decades and translated into ten languages, giving its lines wide reach detached from any citation.
Because the underlying ideas really do echo the Tao Te Ching, casual readers rarely question the Lao Tzu label.
context.pull: An authentically Taoist mood — but a twentieth-century sentence.
